title: Time is greater than space (Evangelii Gaudium 222)
hookLine: start processes rather than seize territory
tomorrow: can you love the planet and ignore the person next to you?

lines: A FIELD OF WHEAT AND WEEDS.
cards: Some weeks you want the whole thing fixed by Friday: the friendship, the grades, the habit, the family mess. One big push, and done.
Pope Francis has a principle for that urge, and its name sounds like physics: time is greater than space.
It sits in Evangelii Gaudium, and he explains it with a farmer whose field comes up wheat, with weeds growing right in among it.

teach.h: LET BOTH GROW UNTIL THE HARVEST.
teach.b: In Jesus's parable, the farmer's servants want to rush out and pull the weeds at once. He tells them no: you'll rip up the wheat too. Let both grow until the harvest.
Francis builds on that. It's the first of four principles he gives for building a people that lives in peace.
Space, in his sense, is ground you can hold right now: a position, a win, control.
Time is the open horizon, where things grow. Putting time first means starting processes rather than possessing spaces.
It lets you work slowly but surely, without being obsessed with quick results, and it helps you bear hard situations and plans that have to change.
Then the opposite mistake: trying to hold everything together in the present, grabbing every space of power and self-assertion, freezing what ought to move. And here's the line worth repeating.
Processes, he says, involve other people, who can carry them on until they bear fruit. A seized space belongs to you. A started process belongs to everyone who joins it.
So patience here isn't doing nothing. The enemy's weeds are real, Francis says, but in the end the goodness of the wheat wins out. You plant something, and trust the harvest to time.

how: Catholic groups who work from Evangelii Gaudium use time is greater than space as a reminder to begin patient, shared work rather than chase quick wins.

games.q: what does “time is greater than space” mean?
o: start slow work that grows, rather than grab ground now
a teaching that the universe is older than the earth
a rule to spend more time in church than elsewhere

games.q: time and space — tap the pairs.
p: ground you can hold right now
the open horizon where things grow
let both grow until the harvest

s: time is greater than space means just wait and do nothing
it means starting processes: planting something and trusting the harvest to time.
Francis uses the parable of the wheat and the weeds for this principle
the weeds are real, he says, and the goodness of the wheat wins out in the end.
this is the only principle Francis offers for building peace

games.q: your friend's parents are splitting up, and you want to fix her whole week: plans every night, a playlist, a group gift. what would putting time first look like?
o: fill every night this week so she's never alone.
start one small, steady thing she can count on, like a weekly walk.
give her space and check back in a month or two.
games.why: Francis says start processes rather than seize spaces: slow, steady work without obsessing over quick results, that others can carry on.

practice: Choose one thing you've wanted to fix in a single push. Then send one short text that starts something slow instead: a standing call, a weekly walk, a first small question.
If you pray, you can offer that seed to God and leave the harvest with him.

wordCard.voice: Time is greater than space. Francis's principle: start something that can grow, rather than grab ground you can hold today.

orig.note: Greek for the weeds sown among the wheat in Matthew 13, the parable Francis uses here.

carryVoice: Hold onto this: start processes, and let other people help carry them. That's the day.
